quizzes.quiz_name: Saqr Academy — Prompt Engineering & Repo Workflow

lessons.lesson_name: Prompt Anatomy: Role, Scope & Hard Limits

questions.question_text: Across the course's build prompts, what pattern consistently limits an agent to only the current feature?
choices: An explicit "Hard limits" or "Do not build X" list naming the other features by ID
Relying on the agent to infer scope from context alone
A single sentence with no explicit boundary
Splitting the app into separate GitHub repos per feature
correct_answer: An explicit "Hard limits" or "Do not build X" list naming the other features by ID
questions.explanation: Nearly every build prompt across the course (e.g. "Only build S3-F1. Do not build S3-F2 or S3-F3.") states the exclusion explicitly rather than trusting the agent to infer it.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of giving an agent a "Read:" list at the top of a prompt (e.g. AGENTS.md, the feature list, the design guide)?
choices: It grounds the agent in the current project state before it acts, instead of relying on chat memory
It is purely decorative and has no functional effect
It forces the agent to summarize each file back to the user first
It replaces the need for a hard-limits section
correct_answer: It grounds the agent in the current project state before it acts, instead of relying on chat memory
questions.explanation: This is the course's core lesson from 'Give Every Agent a System': standards in files travel, standards in a chat thread disappear.

questions.question_text: What is a "done_when" criterion, as used throughout the course's feature lists?
choices: A specific, testable condition that proves a feature is actually complete
A vague aspiration like "the app feels finished"
The date the feature is due
A code comment left in the source file
correct_answer: A specific, testable condition that proves a feature is actually complete
questions.explanation: e.g. "A moved task stays in the new column after page refresh" — a done_when is written so a human can verify it directly in the running app.

questions.question_text: Why does the course's "hard rule" say not to mark a feature's `passes` flag true until done_when is verified?
choices: It stops the agent from confidently reporting work as finished when it isn't
It is required by the GitHub CLI
It prevents merge conflicts
It automatically triggers a deploy
correct_answer: It stops the agent from confidently reporting work as finished when it isn't
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the pre-work concepts lesson: "progress moves on evidence, not on vibes."

questions.question_text: What single-sentence pattern does the course use to correct an agent that has expanded beyond the approved scope?
choices: A short "No" followed by a restatement of the exact approved scope
A long apology followed by a full re-explanation of the whole brief
Silently deleting the extra code without telling the agent
Switching to a different AI model entirely
correct_answer: A short "No" followed by a restatement of the exact approved scope
questions.explanation: Every "Scope correction" / "Reject · Out of scope" prompt in the course follows this same tight, one-or-two-line pattern.

questions.question_text: Why do several prompts explicitly forbid installing new npm packages for drag-and-drop?
choices: To force the agent toward the simplest solution (native browser APIs) instead of adding dependencies
Because npm is not available in the course environment
Because drag-and-drop is never used in any course app
Because it would break the GitHub CLI
correct_answer: To force the agent toward the simplest solution (native browser APIs) instead of adding dependencies
questions.explanation: This constraint appears repeatedly (Founder Sprint Board, Client Pipeline Board, Cloud Task Board) as a way to keep scope and dependencies minimal.

questions.question_text: What is the function of a "Before you build, repeat back the [requirements] in plain English" instruction, seen in several build prompts?
choices: It has the agent confirm its understanding before writing any code, catching misreadings early
It is a formality with no real effect on output quality
It replaces the need for a plan-mode step
It is only used for AI feature prompts
correct_answer: It has the agent confirm its understanding before writing any code, catching misreadings early
questions.explanation: This appears in build prompts as a cheap, early checkpoint against misunderstanding the brief.

questions.question_text: Why do the course's AI-feature prompts (e.g. the Draft follow-up in the Lightweight CRM) specify "no sending — the draft is shown for the user to copy"?
choices: It limits the AI feature's real-world blast radius while still letting students practice building one
Because email sending is technically impossible in Next.js
Because it makes the UI simpler to design
Because Supabase does not support outbound email
correct_answer: It limits the AI feature's real-world blast radius while still letting students practice building one
questions.explanation: This is a deliberate scope constraint — the AI action produces output a human reviews and acts on, rather than an autonomous side effect.

questions.question_text: What do prompts mean when they instruct an agent to "stay within docs/05_Design.md" while building a screen?
choices: Only build the UI elements and actions the design spec already lists — nothing extra
Copy the markdown file's formatting exactly into the component
Ignore the design spec if it conflicts with the PRD
Design the screen from scratch, ignoring any prior spec
correct_answer: Only build the UI elements and actions the design spec already lists — nothing extra
questions.explanation: This is the course's anti-clutter discipline: "Do not add buttons, links, or sections that are not in docs/05_Design.md."

questions.question_text: What structural difference exists between a course prompt's "Reference" block and its "Build"/"Plan" blocks?
choices: A Reference block shows an example the student is told not to paste; the others are meant to be pasted directly
There is no difference — both are pasted identically
Reference blocks are always shorter than one line
Reference blocks are only used for deployment steps
correct_answer: A Reference block shows an example the student is told not to paste; the others are meant to be pasted directly
questions.explanation: e.g. "Reference · AGENTS.md shape — Claude writes this file. You are not pasting it. You are looking at it so you can recognise the shape."

questions.question_text: Why do many prompts specify an exact commit message and PR title rather than leaving them to the agent's judgment?
choices: To keep commit history and PR titles consistent and predictable across every student's repo
Because GitHub CLI requires a fixed message format
Because agents cannot generate commit messages on their own
Because it saves tokens compared to free-form text
correct_answer: To keep commit history and PR titles consistent and predictable across every student's repo
questions.explanation: e.g. "commit message: feat: add S3-F1 task editing / PR title: S3-F1: Edit task title and priority" — specified verbatim in the prompt.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of placeholder text like "[PASTE CLAUDE PLAN]" or "[DESCRIBE FAILURE]" inside a prompt?
choices: It marks where the student inserts fresh, situation-specific content before pasting the prompt
It is a bug that should be removed before use
It tells the agent to generate random text at that point
It indicates an optional section that can be deleted
correct_answer: It marks where the student inserts fresh, situation-specific content before pasting the prompt
questions.explanation: These bracketed placeholders appear throughout the course's plan-review, fix, and correction prompts.

questions.question_text: Why does the course consistently cap instruction-file line counts (e.g. AGENTS.md under 80 lines)?
choices: Long instruction files get reloaded into context on every turn, wasting tokens on repeated content
GitHub rejects files over a certain line count
Word processors cannot render longer files
It is a hard technical limit of the Claude Code tool
correct_answer: Long instruction files get reloaded into context on every turn, wasting tokens on repeated content
questions.explanation: This is the course's explicit "thin files" reasoning, stated in both the Session 3 pre-work and live-class lessons.

questions.question_text: What do the course's escalation prompts (e.g. "Unblock · Email confirmation", "Unblock · Auth redirects") have in common?
choices: They ask the agent for the fastest safe fix to a specific, named blocker, rather than a general troubleshooting request
They always require switching to a different AI tool
They instruct the agent to ignore the blocker and continue
They are only used once per course, never repeated
correct_answer: They ask the agent for the fastest safe fix to a specific, named blocker, rather than a general troubleshooting request
questions.explanation: Each names the exact symptom (e.g. "Supabase email confirmation is blocking test login") so the agent's answer is targeted, not generic.

questions.question_text: Why do several prompts explicitly say "Do not duplicate the PRD" or "Do not paste the feature list into either file" when creating AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md?
choices: To keep each document as a single source of truth instead of copies that can drift out of sync
Because duplicated content crashes the build script
Because AGENTS.md has a strict character limit enforced by Git
Because the PRD is considered confidential
correct_answer: To keep each document as a single source of truth instead of copies that can drift out of sync
questions.explanation: AGENTS.md is meant to route the agent to the right docs, not restate their content — duplication risks the two going out of sync.

lessons.lesson_name: Plan → Build → Verify & the Review Loop

questions.question_text: What is the four-step build loop taught from the very first pre-work lesson?
choices: Plan, Build, Verify, Update progress
Design, Prototype, Test, Launch
Ideate, Code, Deploy, Celebrate
Sketch, Approve, Build, Archive
correct_answer: Plan, Build, Verify, Update progress
questions.explanation: This loop repeats, unchanged in shape, from Session 1's earliest teaching through every later build sprint.

questions.question_text: Why is an agent switched into a dedicated "Plan mode" before a feature is built, rather than building immediately?
choices: So the student can review the intended approach before any files are changed
Plan mode is required by the GitHub CLI to create a branch
It makes the agent run faster
It is only used for AI-feature prompts, never regular features
correct_answer: So the student can review the intended approach before any files are changed
questions.explanation: Plan-mode prompts consistently include "Do not edit files" — the plan is reviewed and approved before Build mode starts.

questions.question_text: What is the core reason the course insists a different agent (or a fresh thread) reviews a plan or PR than the one that wrote it?
choices: The same context that produced the work is poorly positioned to catch its own mistakes
Reviewing in the same thread is technically impossible
It is required to keep GitHub CLI authenticated
Fresh threads run faster than long-running ones
correct_answer: The same context that produced the work is poorly positioned to catch its own mistakes
questions.explanation: Stated as a hard rule in Session 3: "Do not let the same context approve itself."

questions.question_text: In the course's plan-review prompts, what three verdicts can a reviewing agent return?
choices: APPROVE, APPROVE WITH NOTES, BLOCK
PASS, FAIL, PENDING
YES, NO, MAYBE
MERGE, HOLD, REJECT
correct_answer: APPROVE, APPROVE WITH NOTES, BLOCK
questions.explanation: This exact three-way scale recurs across every plan-review prompt in the course.

questions.question_text: What severity scale does the course's code-review (post-build, pre-merge) prompts use?
choices: P0 (blocks merge) through P3 (optional polish)
1-star through 5-star
Low, Medium, High only
Blocker, Nice-to-have
correct_answer: P0 (blocks merge) through P3 (optional polish)
questions.explanation: Introduced in Session 3's Codex code-review prompt and reused in later review prompts.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of a dedicated "UX gate" prompt, distinct from the plan/architecture review?
choices: It checks a screen specifically for one job, one primary action, and nothing smuggled in — a different failure mode than scope or bugs
It replaces the need for a code review entirely
It only runs after the app is deployed to production
It checks page-load speed and nothing else
correct_answer: It checks a screen specifically for one job, one primary action, and nothing smuggled in — a different failure mode than scope or bugs
questions.explanation: The course is explicit: "Architecture review and UX review are not the same thing."

questions.question_text: What must happen if a UX gate returns BLOCK, per the course's rule?
choices: The screen spec must be fixed and the gate re-run before building continues
The finding is noted but building continues anyway
The whole feature is cancelled permanently
The student overrides it and proceeds regardless
correct_answer: The screen spec must be fixed and the gate re-run before building continues
questions.explanation: "If BLOCK, do not build until the screen spec is fixed" — this appears verbatim in multiple UX-gate prompts.

questions.question_text: In the sprint loop, what step directly follows a successful Build step?
choices: Verify — the student checks the done_when condition themselves in the running app
Immediately merging to main with no review
Deleting the feature branch
Writing the PRD
correct_answer: Verify — the student checks the done_when condition themselves in the running app
questions.explanation: Verification is explicitly a student action, not something the agent self-certifies.

questions.question_text: Why does a "Fix" prompt (e.g. "Fix S3-F1", "Fix workflow failure") typically include a "[DESCRIBE FAILURE]" placeholder rather than just saying "fix the bug"?
choices: A concrete symptom description keeps the fix targeted instead of triggering a broad, unscoped rewrite
The agent cannot fix anything without an exact stack trace
It is required syntax for the GitHub CLI
It prevents the agent from creating a new branch
correct_answer: A concrete symptom description keeps the fix targeted instead of triggering a broad, unscoped rewrite
questions.explanation: These prompts also add "Fix only [X]" to keep the fix scoped to the one broken feature.

questions.question_text: What is the mini-sprint protocol's five-step shape, as taught in Session 2?
choices: Plan mode, Review the plan, Build, Verify, Update tracking
Design, Build, Ship, Market, Support
Idea, Prototype, Test, Launch, Iterate
Read, Write, Test, Deploy, Document
correct_answer: Plan mode, Review the plan, Build, Verify, Update tracking
questions.explanation: "Learn it once, apply it four times" — this shape repeats identically for each of the four Session 2 features.

questions.question_text: What happens to a feature's tracking docs (feature list JSON and progress.md) only after verification succeeds?
choices: Its `passes` flag is set to true and the change is recorded
They are deleted to save space
They are locked from future edits permanently
Nothing — tracking docs are updated before verification, not after
correct_answer: Its `passes` flag is set to true and the change is recorded
questions.explanation: "Do not set passes to true unless done_when is actually satisfied" is the recurring hard rule.

questions.question_text: Why does the course use a separate agent thread for reviewing a PR rather than continuing the same conversation that built the feature?
choices: A fresh thread has no prior bias toward defending decisions it already made
Continuing the same thread is technically disallowed by GitHub CLI
Fresh threads are billed differently
It is purely a stylistic choice with no functional benefit
correct_answer: A fresh thread has no prior bias toward defending decisions it already made
questions.explanation: This is the same principle behind the "same context cannot approve itself" hard rule, applied to PR review specifically.

questions.question_text: What review lens does the Security Lab's "Fix Verifier" prompt add on top of the course's normal code-review checks?
choices: Confirming the original exploit no longer works and no new privilege or data exposure was introduced
Checking only that the code compiles without errors
Checking that the commit message follows the correct format
Checking that the PR description is grammatically correct
correct_answer: Confirming the original exploit no longer works and no new privilege or data exposure was introduced
questions.explanation: This extends the plan/code review pattern specifically to security fixes, closing the loop with a re-run of the original reproduction steps.

questions.question_text: What does the course define a "branch" as?
choices: A parallel copy of your code where you try a change without breaking the main version
A backup of the entire repository stored offline
A separate GitHub account for each feature
A folder inside node_modules
correct_answer: A parallel copy of your code where you try a change without breaking the main version
questions.explanation: This is the exact vocabulary-card definition from the Session 1 pre-work lesson.

questions.question_text: What is a "Pull Request" defined as in the course?
choices: The proposal to bring a branch's change in, opened so it can be reviewed before it merges
A request sent to GitHub support for account help
An automatic nightly backup of the repo
A request to delete an old branch
correct_answer: The proposal to bring a branch's change in, opened so it can be reviewed before it merges
questions.explanation: Exact vocabulary-card definition, reused unchanged from Session 1 through Session 4.

questions.question_text: What naming convention do the course's feature branches consistently follow?
choices: feature/<feature-id>-<short-kebab-case-description>
A random UUID with no readable meaning
The student's first name plus a date stamp
main-v2, main-v3, main-v4, incrementing
correct_answer: feature/<feature-id>-<short-kebab-case-description>
questions.explanation: e.g. feature/S3-F1-edit-task-title-priority, feature/S3-H2-contact-detail-ai-followup — always this shape.

questions.question_text: What merge strategy is specified across nearly every "Merge" prompt in the course?
choices: Squash merge
Rebase and merge
A plain merge commit
Fast-forward only, with squash disabled
correct_answer: Squash merge
questions.explanation: Every merge prompt from Session 2 onward specifies squash merge, keeping main's history to one commit per feature.

questions.question_text: What two actions consistently follow a squash merge in the course's prompts?
choices: Switch back to main and pull the latest
Delete the entire repository
Immediately deploy to production with no verification
Create a new branch with the same name
correct_answer: Switch back to main and pull the latest
questions.explanation: This keeps the local main in sync before the next feature branch is created.

questions.question_text: Why does the course say "Do not merge the PR yet" immediately after opening one?
choices: A merge should only happen after a separate review has passed
GitHub CLI cannot merge and open a PR in the same session
It is illegal to merge your own PR on GitHub
Merging immediately deletes the branch
correct_answer: A merge should only happen after a separate review has passed
questions.explanation: Opening the PR and reviewing it are treated as separate steps precisely to prevent self-approval.

questions.question_text: What CLI tool does the course use for creating repos, opening PRs, and merging — instead of the GitHub website?
choices: GitHub CLI (gh)
git push --force
The Vercel dashboard
cURL against the GitHub REST API by hand
correct_answer: GitHub CLI (gh)
questions.explanation: "Use GitHub CLI as the default path" appears throughout, with browser-based fallback only if authentication blocks the CLI.

questions.question_text: What is a "baseline commit," as used before Session 3's feature-branch work begins?
choices: A clean commit of just the workflow-setup files, with no app code changes, so every branch starts from the same starting point
The very first commit ever made to the repository
A commit made directly on the deployed production branch
A commit that reverts all previous work
correct_answer: A clean commit of just the workflow-setup files, with no app code changes, so every branch starts from the same starting point
questions.explanation: This isolates instruction-file and feature-list setup from any actual product code before branching starts.

questions.question_text: What does the course instruct an agent to do if it encounters uncommitted changes at the start of a session, before touching anything?
choices: Explain what they are in plain English and wait for the student's decision
Silently discard them and start fresh
Automatically commit them with a generic message
Force-push over them
correct_answer: Explain what they are in plain English and wait for the student's decision
questions.explanation: "Do not discard anything. Tell me whether they look like completed work, generated files, or accidental changes. Wait for my decision."

questions.question_text: How does the course define "Code review" on its vocabulary card?
choices: A second pass on a change before it merges, by a person or another agent
The act of writing the original code
A test suite that runs automatically on every commit
A meeting where the whole team discusses the roadmap
correct_answer: A second pass on a change before it merges, by a person or another agent
questions.explanation: Exact vocabulary-card definition from the pre-work lesson.

questions.question_text: What does the course explicitly forbid an agent from doing to git history without approval?
choices: Rewriting it (e.g. after a leaked secret) without explicit human sign-off
Creating any new branches at all
Writing commit messages in English
Pushing to a feature branch
correct_answer: Rewriting it (e.g. after a leaked secret) without explicit human sign-off
questions.explanation: "Do not rewrite git history without explicit approval" is stated directly in the leaked-secret remediation prompt.

questions.question_text: What GitHub CLI-related fallback pattern recurs whenever authentication or permissions might block a CLI action?
choices: The agent explains the exact human authorization step needed and waits
The agent silently switches to the GitHub website and continues unattended
The agent skips that step entirely with no explanation
The agent asks the student for their GitHub password
correct_answer: The agent explains the exact human authorization step needed and waits
questions.explanation: This exact fallback phrasing ("tell me the exact human authorization step needed and wait") recurs for GitHub CLI, Vercel CLI, and Supabase CLI blockers alike.

questions.question_text: What does "Merge" mean, per the course's vocabulary card?
choices: Accepting a pull request and bringing the change into the main code
Deleting a branch after it is no longer needed
Combining two unrelated repositories into one
Running a database migration
correct_answer: Accepting a pull request and bringing the change into the main code
questions.explanation: Exact vocabulary-card definition.

questions.question_text: Why might a student be told to "stop after PR creation and review" rather than merging, if time is short?
choices: A reviewed-but-unmerged PR is still meaningful progress that can be completed later, without rushing the merge decision
Merging always fails if done under time pressure
GitHub CLI has a daily merge quota
PRs automatically expire after 24 hours
correct_answer: A reviewed-but-unmerged PR is still meaningful progress that can be completed later, without rushing the merge decision
questions.explanation: This appears in the Session 3 live-class agent-switch drill as an explicit time-management fallback.

questions.question_text: What key does virtually every Supabase-setup prompt in the course explicitly forbid requesting or using?
choices: The Supabase secret key (service_role)
The publishable/anon key
The project's URL
The project's region identifier
correct_answer: The Supabase secret key (service_role)
questions.explanation: "Never ask for or use the Supabase secret key" recurs from Session 2 through the Security Lab.

questions.question_text: What does Row Level Security (RLS) enforce, as tested throughout the course's prompts?
choices: Authenticated users can only select, insert, update, and delete their own rows
All users can read all data but not modify it
Only the app's admin can log in at all
Data is encrypted at rest, regardless of who queries it
correct_answer: Authenticated users can only select, insert, update, and delete their own rows
questions.explanation: This exact RLS scope is requested in every Supabase-setup prompt, from Cloud Task Board through the Lightweight CRM.

questions.question_text: What file must stay out of GitHub, per repeated instructions across the course?
choices: .env.local
package.json
README.md
next.config.js
correct_answer: .env.local
questions.explanation: Checked explicitly in readiness-check prompts (".env.local is ignored by git") from Session 2 onward.

questions.question_text: What must happen first, per the course, if a secret is discovered committed to a repo?
choices: Stop all feature work and create a safe remediation plan before doing anything else
Immediately force-push a fix to erase it from history
Wait until the next scheduled release to address it
Delete the GitHub repository entirely
correct_answer: Stop all feature work and create a safe remediation plan before doing anything else
questions.explanation: "A leaked secret is not a normal bug" — this is treated as a dedicated, escalated prompt path in both Session 4 and the Security Lab.

questions.question_text: What does the course recommend regarding an exposed secret, citing GitHub's own guidance?
choices: Revoke or rotate the exposed secret first — history cleanup is a separate decision
Ignore it unless the app has real users
Only rotate the key if asked to by a client
Delete the commit but keep the same secret value active
correct_answer: Revoke or rotate the exposed secret first — history cleanup is a separate decision
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the Release Readiness lesson's leaked-secret remediation prompt.

questions.question_text: In the safety-audit prompt, what two environment variables should the public/browser Supabase client use?
choices: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY (or legacy anon key)
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and DATABASE_URL
OPENAI_API_KEY and VERCEL_TOKEN
GITHUB_TOKEN and NPM_TOKEN
correct_answer: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY (or legacy anon key)
questions.explanation: This exact pair is checked by the Session 4 safety-gate audit prompt.

questions.question_text: Where must an LLM API key live, per the Lightweight CRM's AI-feature constraints?
choices: A server-side environment variable, never in client code, never committed
In the component's props, passed from the server on every render
Hardcoded as a fallback in case the environment variable is missing
In the Supabase publishable key field
correct_answer: A server-side environment variable, never in client code, never committed
questions.explanation: This exact constraint is repeated across the bootstrap prompt, the build prompt, and the review prompt for S3-H2.

questions.question_text: What must production environment variables exist on before a deploy is considered release-ready?
choices: Vercel
The student's local .env.local file only
A shared Google Doc
The GitHub repository's README
correct_answer: Vercel
questions.explanation: Every deploy prompt from Session 2 through Session 4 checks that required env vars exist in Vercel before a production deploy.

questions.question_text: What does the course's Security Lab call it when a security check relies only on hiding a UI element?
choices: A suggestion, not security
A best practice
Defense in depth
A zero-day mitigation
correct_answer: A suggestion, not security
questions.explanation: "A hidden button does not mean a closed endpoint" — the lab insists on server-side or database-layer enforcement.

questions.question_text: What manual test does the course use to verify RLS is actually working, rather than trusting the agent's report?
choices: Log in as two different test users and try to access each other's records directly through the API
Read the RLS policy source code and assume it is correct if it compiles
Ask the agent "is RLS enabled?" and accept a yes/no answer
Check whether the login page has a password field
correct_answer: Log in as two different test users and try to access each other's records directly through the API
questions.explanation: This hands-on cross-user test appears in both the Session 4 safety gate and the Security Lab's Module 03 checkpoint.

questions.question_text: What fallback does the course specify when Supabase CLI setup is blocked?
choices: A generated SQL script the student pastes into the Supabase dashboard SQL Editor
Skipping the database entirely for that feature
Switching the whole project to Firebase
Asking a classmate to run the CLI on their machine
correct_answer: A generated SQL script the student pastes into the Supabase dashboard SQL Editor
questions.explanation: This CLI-first, dashboard-fallback pattern is consistent from Session 2's Cloud Task Board through the Lightweight CRM homework.

questions.question_text: What does the course's forbidden-scope list consistently exclude regarding admin or role-based access?
choices: Building new database tables or admin dashboards unless required to fix a real release blocker
Any use of Supabase Auth whatsoever
Deploying to Vercel with environment variables set
Writing a PRD before building
correct_answer: Building new database tables or admin dashboards unless required to fix a real release blocker
questions.explanation: Session 4 explicitly restricts new tables/admin surfaces to only when a genuine release blocker requires them.

questions.question_text: What kind of environment variable check appears at the very start of Session 4's readiness check prompt?
choices: Confirming .env.local is ignored by git
Confirming the Vercel account has billing enabled
Confirming the student has read every prior lesson
Confirming the GitHub repo is set to private
correct_answer: Confirming .env.local is ignored by git
questions.explanation: This check runs before any release-gate work begins, alongside confirming AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and the feature list exist.

questions.question_text: What is the course's stated default rule about how an agent should complete a task, whenever possible?
choices: Use the CLI before asking for manual browser/dashboard steps
Always ask the student to do it manually first
Use the browser dashboard by default, CLI only as backup
Avoid CLI tools entirely in favor of GUIs
correct_answer: Use the CLI before asking for manual browser/dashboard steps
questions.explanation: This is one of the course's global "Saqr Academy Working Agreements," applied consistently from Session 2 onward.

questions.question_text: Which three CLI tools recur most often across the course's build, deploy, and setup prompts?
choices: GitHub CLI, Vercel CLI, Supabase CLI
Docker CLI, kubectl, Terraform
npm, Yarn, pnpm
curl, wget, ssh
correct_answer: GitHub CLI, Vercel CLI, Supabase CLI
questions.explanation: These three appear in nearly every session's tool-check and deploy prompts.

questions.question_text: What must a readiness-check prompt do if a required tool or file is missing?
choices: Explain the exact blocker and wait — not edit files, create branches, or deploy
Automatically install whatever is missing without asking
Proceed anyway and hope for the best
Abandon the session and restart from scratch
correct_answer: Explain the exact blocker and wait — not edit files, create branches, or deploy
questions.explanation: Every session's opening "Tool & project check" prompt explicitly forbids taking action beyond diagnosis if something's missing.

questions.question_text: What CLI command does the course use to check whether GitHub CLI is authenticated?
choices: gh auth status
gh whoami
gh check
gh login --status
correct_answer: gh auth status
questions.explanation: Used consistently in every tool-readiness check across the course.

questions.question_text: What CLI command does the course use to check whether Vercel CLI is authenticated?
choices: vercel whoami
vercel auth status
vercel check
vercel me
correct_answer: vercel whoami
questions.explanation: This command returning a username is treated as the pass condition.

questions.question_text: What is the course's stated fallback rule when browser-only or manual dashboard steps are truly required?
choices: They are fallback paths only — used when CLI authentication, permissions, or service limits block the agent
They should always be used instead of the CLI for reliability
They are never allowed under any circumstance
They replace the CLI entirely starting in Session 3
correct_answer: They are fallback paths only — used when CLI authentication, permissions, or service limits block the agent
questions.explanation: Stated as an explicit "Operating principle" in multiple homework lessons.

questions.question_text: Why does the course prefer `npx supabase` or a local dev dependency over a global npm install for the Supabase CLI?
choices: It avoids polluting the student's global environment and keeps the tool version pinned per-project
Global installs are technically impossible on Windows
npx is required by GitHub Actions
It makes deployment to Vercel faster
correct_answer: It avoids polluting the student's global environment and keeps the tool version pinned per-project
questions.explanation: "Use npx supabase or a local dev dependency. Do not use global npm install for Supabase CLI" appears in multiple setup prompts.

questions.question_text: What must a deploy prompt confirm about the working tree before a production deploy?
choices: That git status is clean
That the local .env.local file has been deleted
That the student has manually tested every API route by hand
That the app has no open GitHub issues
correct_answer: That git status is clean
questions.explanation: Nearly every deploy prompt from Session 2 through 4 checks git status is clean before deploying.

questions.question_text: What information does an agent give the student after successfully deploying, per the course's deploy prompts?
choices: The live URL and a short verification checklist
Only a success/failure boolean with no further detail
The full server logs with no summary
A link to the Vercel billing page
correct_answer: The live URL and a short verification checklist
questions.explanation: Every deploy prompt in the course ends by asking for the live URL plus steps to verify it.

questions.question_text: What is the exact required content of the "reject out-of-scope CLI package suggestion" pattern regarding drag-and-drop?
choices: Use native browser drag-and-drop plus fallback move buttons — no installed libraries
Install the most popular npm drag-and-drop library available
Skip drag-and-drop and use only keyboard navigation
Use a paid third-party drag-and-drop SaaS
correct_answer: Use native browser drag-and-drop plus fallback move buttons — no installed libraries
questions.explanation: This constraint recurs verbatim (or near-verbatim) across every board app in the course.

questions.question_text: What is the course's default assumption about who runs terminal commands like `git status` or `vercel whoami`?
choices: The agent runs them, and the student authorises/verifies the outcome
The student always types every command by hand
Neither — these commands are avoided entirely
A dedicated DevOps teaching assistant runs them
correct_answer: The agent runs them, and the student authorises/verifies the outcome
questions.explanation: "If the agent can carry out a task, the student should not be asked to do it manually" is a course-wide operating principle.

questions.question_text: When a database migration is required mid-build (e.g. for the Lightweight CRM's AI feature), what does the course ask the agent to do before applying it?
choices: Create the smallest safe migration and explain it before applying
Apply it immediately without explanation to save time
Skip the migration and use a JSON file instead
Ask a different student to review it first
correct_answer: Create the smallest safe migration and explain it before applying
questions.explanation: This appears in the S3-H2 build prompt as a specific safeguard around mid-build schema changes.

questions.question_text: What is the Security Lab's threat-model prompt explicitly told NOT to do yet?
choices: Fix anything — it should only produce a prioritized map of risk
Read the database schema
Name any attack surfaces
List external services and secrets
correct_answer: Fix anything — it should only produce a prioritized map of risk
questions.explanation: "Do not fix anything yet. Produce a prioritized threat model with file references where possible."

questions.question_text: What six things must the threat-model prompt return?
choices: Sensitive assets, roles/trust boundaries, external services/secrets, attack surfaces, top 10 abuse cases, highest-risk flows to test
A complete rewrite of the authentication system
A cost estimate for a security consultant
Just a single pass/fail security score
correct_answer: Sensitive assets, roles/trust boundaries, external services/secrets, attack surfaces, top 10 abuse cases, highest-risk flows to test
questions.explanation: This is the exact six-item return list from the "Prompt · Threat model" block.

questions.question_text: What seven checks does the Supabase audit prompt run through?
choices: RLS enabled everywhere, cross-user policy checks, admin-table exposure, no service_role in frontend, minimal anon/authenticated permissions, owner-based storage access, cross-user access tests exist
Only whether Supabase billing is set up correctly
Only whether the database has any tables at all
Only whether migrations are named consistently
correct_answer: RLS enabled everywhere, cross-user policy checks, admin-table exposure, no service_role in frontend, minimal anon/authenticated permissions, owner-based storage access, cross-user access tests exist
questions.explanation: This is the exact seven-point checklist inside the "Prompt · Supabase audit" block.

questions.question_text: What eight vulnerability classes does the API security review prompt look for?
choices: Missing auth, missing ownership/role checks, client-side-only authorization, ID tampering, missing validation, unsafe error messages, missing rate limits, unverified webhooks
Only slow response times
Only missing TypeScript types
Only outdated npm dependencies
correct_answer: Missing auth, missing ownership/role checks, client-side-only authorization, ID tampering, missing validation, unsafe error messages, missing rate limits, unverified webhooks
questions.explanation: This is the exact eight-item list in the "Prompt · API security review" block.

questions.question_text: What six abuse categories does the AI abuse test prompt try to identify?
choices: Overriding instructions, extracting hidden prompts, cross-user data via AI responses, unsafe tool calls, revealing secrets/logs, excessive cost/background work
Only whether the AI responds in the correct language
Only whether the AI's response time is under 2 seconds
Only whether the AI uses polite phrasing
correct_answer: Overriding instructions, extracting hidden prompts, cross-user data via AI responses, unsafe tool calls, revealing secrets/logs, excessive cost/background work
questions.explanation: This is the exact six-item list from "Prompt · AI abuse test."

questions.question_text: What seven attack categories does the Agentic Pen Test prompt cover?
choices: Unauthenticated access, cross-user data access, ID tampering, file/storage abuse, privilege bypass, prompt injection, replay/repeated requests
Only DNS misconfiguration
Only outdated SSL certificates
Only CSS injection
correct_answer: Unauthenticated access, cross-user data access, ID tampering, file/storage abuse, privilege bypass, prompt injection, replay/repeated requests
questions.explanation: This is the exact seven-item list from "Prompt · Agentic pen test."

questions.question_text: What environment boundary does the Agentic Pen Test prompt explicitly enforce?
choices: Stay within the local/test environment; do not attack third-party systems
Test only against the production URL for realism
Test any publicly accessible website for practice
No boundary is specified — students choose their own target
correct_answer: Stay within the local/test environment; do not attack third-party systems
questions.explanation: This restriction is stated in bold in the lesson and repeated inside the prompt itself.

questions.question_text: What five things does the Fix Verifier prompt confirm?
choices: Exploit no longer works, fix is server-side/database-layer, UI wasn't the only change, regression tests cover it, no new exposure was introduced
Only that the code passes a linter
Only that the commit message is well-formatted
Only that the PR has at least one comment
correct_answer: Exploit no longer works, fix is server-side/database-layer, UI wasn't the only change, regression tests cover it, no new exposure was introduced
questions.explanation: This is the exact five-item confirmation list from "Prompt · Fix verifier."

questions.question_text: What three possible verdicts does the Fix Verifier prompt return?
choices: Fixed, partially fixed, not fixed
Pass, fail, retry
Critical, high, low
Approved, blocked, pending
correct_answer: Fixed, partially fixed, not fixed
questions.explanation: This three-way verdict is distinct from the earlier APPROVE/BLOCK plan-review scale, reflecting a different review purpose.

questions.question_text: What ten sections does the Final Audit Report prompt require?
choices: Scope, auth/authz findings, Supabase/RLS findings, API findings, AI-specific findings, secrets/env findings, storage findings, fixed today, still open, recommended next actions
Only an executive summary with no detail
Only a bulleted list of every file changed
Only a timeline of when each audit module was run
correct_answer: Scope, auth/authz findings, Supabase/RLS findings, API findings, AI-specific findings, secrets/env findings, storage findings, fixed today, still open, recommended next actions
questions.explanation: This exact ten-item structure is specified in "Prompt · Final audit report."

questions.question_text: What severity scale does the Final Audit Report prompt specify?
choices: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational
P0 through P3
Red, Amber, Green
1 through 10 numeric score
correct_answer: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational
questions.explanation: Every finding in the report needs evidence, impact, and a recommended fix, scored on this five-point scale.

questions.question_text: Why does the Security Lab tell students not to trust an agent's own severity rating on a pen-test finding without checking it?
choices: Because the student, not the agent, is ultimately accountable for judging real-world risk
Because agents cannot assign severity ratings at all
Because severity ratings are randomly generated
Because only Codex is allowed to assign severity, never Claude
correct_answer: Because the student, not the agent, is ultimately accountable for judging real-world risk
questions.explanation: This mirrors the course's broader "student directs, agent executes, student verifies" principle applied to security work specifically.
